program.name: SGL-001 development program
program.current_formulation_hypothesis: Intranasal mesenchymal-stromal-cell-derived small-EV preparation with defined identity, purity, dose, and a mechanism-relevant potency assay; therapeutic cargo remains to be selected.
program.largest_unresolved_risk: Intranasal CNS exposure observed in rodents may not translate to larger species or humans.
program.next_proposed_action: Program lead to assemble Stage-1 package (GLP large-animal intranasal biodistribution/tox, three GMP-like scale-up runs with draft specs and stability, validated potency/orthogonal QC plan, and regulator briefing) and request pre-IND/Scientific Advice in two jurisdictions; 3-month timeline.

claims.statement: Rodent intranasal biodistribution data alone are insufficient to predict reproducible intact-EV CNS exposure in larger species without matching intact-EV assays and bridging controls.
claims.rationale: Cross-species biodistribution literature and characterization guidance indicate limited translatability absent orthogonal intact-EV analytics and controlled bridging studies.

claims.statement: Rodent intranasal MSC-derived EVs show reproducible benefit in injury models and justify further candidate-defining and translational studies but do not by themselves demonstrate intact-EV CNS exposure in larger species.
claims.rationale: Multiple rodent studies show functional benefit; however, these data do not quantify intact-EV CNS exposure or cross-species translation.

claims.statement: Current materials do not demonstrate characterized source-cell MCB/WCB or scalable, reproducible production sufficient to support advancing a specific intranasal formulation.
claims.rationale: No MCB/WCB, validated scale-up or reproducibility data provided; MISEV recommends defined production controls and reporting.

claims.statement: An orthogonal QC panel (particles, protein, lipid markers per MISEV), validated intact-EV assays (LLOQ, specificity, precision), and stability-indicating, mechanism-linked potency assays are required before formulation advancement.
claims.rationale: MISEV2023 consensus supports orthogonal characterization and transparent release/assay criteria to de-risk identity and potency claims.

claims.statement: Intranasal CNS delivery of EVs does not reliably translate across species: one macaque study found negligible brain uptake and no reliable CSF signal after intranasal administration of Expi293F-derived EVs.
claims.rationale: This directly limits extrapolation from rodent localization studies; differences in EV source, formulation, labeling, dosing, and administration remain possible explanations.

changes.summary: No material scientific change. Re-evaluated the pending candidate-definition decision and retained it for human review; the next action is to review the existing staged candidate-definition and quantitative biodistribution package before committing program resources.

evidence.title: Treatment of brain inflammatory diseases by delivering exosome encapsulated anti-inflammatory drugs from the nasal region to the brain
evidence.excerpt: Curated summary: in mouse models, intranasal exosomes carrying curcumin or a STAT3 inhibitor were reported to reach brain microglia and improve model-specific inflammatory or tumor outcomes. These findings are preclinical and formulation-specific.

metadata.model_or_indication: mouse brain inflammation and glioma models

evidence.title: Intranasal MSC-derived A1-exosomes ease inflammation, and prevent abnormal neurogenesis and memory dysfunction after status epilepticus
evidence.excerpt: Curated summary: after status epilepticus in young mice, intranasally administered human MSC-derived EVs were reported in the hippocampus and were associated with reduced neuronal loss and inflammation and preservation of neurogenesis and cognitive or memory outcomes versus vehicle.

evidence.title: Extracellular vesicles from immortalized mesenchymal stromal cells protect against neonatal hypoxic-ischemic brain injury
evidence.excerpt: Curated summary: repeated intranasal EV administration after hypoxic-ischemic injury reduced brain tissue atrophy in neonatal mice; EVs from a clonal immortalized MSC line and primary MSCs showed comparable effects. The study frames source-cell consistency and scale as translational considerations.

evidence.title: Minimal information for studies of extracellular vesicles (MISEV2023): From basic to advanced approaches
evidence.excerpt: Curated summary: the ISEV consensus identifies continuing challenges in EV nomenclature, separation from non-vesicular particles, characterization, functional studies, production reporting, and in-vivo evaluation; it recommends transparent, orthogonal characterization and appropriate controls.

evidence.title: Pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of extracellular vesicles administered intravenously and intranasally to Macaca nemestrina
evidence.excerpt: Curated summary: reporter-labeled Expi293F-derived EVs administered intranasally to macaques were not reliably detected above background in CSF, showed negligible brain uptake, and were strongly retained in nasal lavage. EV source, formulation, labeling, administration, and species may affect generalizability.

hypotheses.statement: Advancing an intranasal formulation into high-confidence delivery and cross-species PK/PD testing requires completion of a defined CMC/analytics/formulation compatibility gating package.
hypotheses.rationale: To ensure observed in vivo signal is attributable to intact EV and is reproducible across lots/species, the program must meet orthogonal analytical and process reproducibility criteria before bridging studies.
hypotheses.test_plan: Stage 1 completion criteria: MCB/WCB produced; orthogonal QC panel defined and assays fit-for-purpose validated (LLOQ, specificity, precision); stability-indicating potency assay correlated to an in vivo PD endpoint; reproducible release/stability/potency across ≥3 GMP-like batches; formulation/device compatibility with intact-EV recovery demonstrated ex vivo and in vivo (controls included).

risks.title: Cross-species translation uncertainty for intranasal intact-EV CNS exposure
risks.description: Rodent intranasal biodistribution may not predict large-species/NHP CNS exposure for intact EV; device and formulation interactions may differ by species.
risks.mitigation: Require ex vivo nasal recovery and rodent intact-EV-specific PK with controls prior to any large-species study; predefine bridging acceptance criteria and include disrupted-EV and free-label controls in all in vivo studies.

risks.title: Insufficient CMC/analytics to establish intact-EV identity, potency, and lot-to-lot reproducibility
risks.description: Lack of MCB/WCB, orthogonal QC, validated potency/stability assays, and scale-up reproducibility may produce misleading in vitro and in vivo results and block regulatory acceptance.
risks.mitigation: Execute Stage 1 actions: generate MCB/WCB, define/validate orthogonal assays, produce representative GMP-like batches, and document stability/potency reproducibility. Escalate assay development resourcing if timelines slip.

risks.title: Model generalizability from injury models to cognition/aging endpoints
risks.description: Efficacy evidence is from acute/injury rodent models; relevance to cognition/aging indications is unproven.
risks.mitigation: Defer indication-specific efficacy studies until biodistribution/PD linkage is demonstrated; design follow-on efficacy models that reflect intended clinical endpoints.

claims.statement: Intranasally administered EV preparations have been reported to reach CNS compartments or CNS-resident cells in multiple mouse studies.
Intranasal EV treatment was associated with improved inflammatory, histologic, or functional outcomes in several rodent CNS injury or disease models.

A clonal immortalized MSC source produced EVs with activity comparable to primary MSC-EVs in one neonatal mouse hypoxic-ischemic injury study, suggesting a testable route to reduce source heterogeneity during scale-up.

EV development requires controlled production, separation, identity and purity characterization, functional testing, and transparent reporting because EV preparations are heterogeneous and may contain non-vesicular co-isolates.

Intranasal CNS delivery of EVs does not reliably translate across species: one macaque study found negligible brain uptake and no reliable CSF signal after intranasal administration of Expi293F-derived EVs.

hypothesis.statement: An intranasal MSC-derived small-EV formulation with controlled identity, purity, dose, and potency attributes can achieve reproducible CNS exposure and a neuroregeneration-relevant pharmacodynamic signal in a cognition or aging model, but advancement should be gated on quantitative biodistribution and translation-oriented acceptance criteria.
hypothesis.whatChanged: No material scientific change. Re-evaluated the pending candidate-definition decision and retained it for human review; the next action is to review the existing staged candidate-definition and quantitative biodistribution package before committing program resources.

critique.strongestObjection: Authorization would be premature if interpreted as approval of a fixed product or efficacy program: the local evidence supports a gated learning package, not a final source-cell, purification process, dose, potency specification, exposure threshold, or clinical indication.
assumptionsChallenged: The evidence does not compare candidate-like SGL-001 formulations under a common manufacturing and analytical framework.
Rodent biological activity does not establish clinically relevant CNS exposure or human efficacy.
The macaque result materially weakens unqualified extrapolation of rodent intranasal delivery findings.
translationalConcerns: The hypothesis is plausible enough to test but remains highly sensitive to EV source, preparation purity, label artifacts, disease-model permeability, nasal retention, dose normalization, and cross-species anatomy. Rodent efficacy cannot establish that SGL-001 reaches a clinically relevant human CNS compartment or will benefit patients.
experimentalConfounders: Demonstrate that measured CNS signal represents intact candidate-associated EV exposure rather than free label, co-isolates, or secondary biological effects.
Define product identity, purity, dose units, stability, and a mechanism-relevant potency assay before interpreting efficacy reproducibility.
Use a staged translational plan because the macaque biodistribution result conflicts with assuming that rodent intranasal brain uptake will generalize to humans.
falsificationConditions: Compare a characterized candidate formulation with vehicle, free-label, and disrupted-EV controls; quantify intact-EV-associated exposure across CNS, nasal, pulmonary, and systemic compartments over time; pair exposure with a predefined neuroregeneration-relevant pharmacodynamic assay, then evaluate cognitive function in an aging-relevant model only if prospectively defined exposure, reproducibility, and safety criteria are met.

decision.question: Should SGL-001 advance into broad cognition/neuroregeneration efficacy development now?
decision.recommendation: Do not advance into broad cognition/neuroregeneration efficacy development yet; propose a gated candidate-definition and quantitative biodistribution/pharmacology package for human approval.
decision.rationale: Multiple rodent studies justify continued preclinical evaluation, but the non-human-primate result makes CNS delivery translation the largest unresolved risk, and EV identity, purity, dose, and potency must be controlled before efficacy can be attributed to a reproducible SGL-001 product.

recentReviews.matter_question: What minimum source-cell, EV identity, cargo, and release definition is required before SGL-001 can be treated as a candidate-like product?
recentReviews.strongest_case_for: Preclinical rodent studies show repeated intranasal MSC-derived EV dosing can reduce injury-associated pathology and functional deficits (Hermann neonatal HI plus earlier intranasal EV studies), and the ISEV/MISEV2023 consensus provides a clear set of requirements for orthogonal EV characterization, functional controls, and reporting that define what candidate-level CMC and quality work should cover.
recentReviews.strongest_case_against: The proposed gate and minimum-definition plan assumes that (a) intranasal intact‑EV CNS delivery observed in rodents will be predictive for larger species/humans and (b) a candidate-like product can be meaningfully specified (release limits, potency assay) prior to selecting therapeutic cargo/mechanism. The primary objection is that cross‑species delivery uncertainty and the unspecified cargo/potency approach make the recommended candidate-definition and go/no‑go criteria premature and potentially uninformative for translational decision‑making.
recentReviews.determination: Approve a mandatory two-stage candidate-definition and biodistribution gate before treating SGL-001 as a candidate-like product: (1) finalize source-cell choice and establish MCB/WCB; define orthogonal identity/purity QC panel and draft release specifications; develop a fit-for-purpose potency assay concept in parallel with small-scale process development; (2) execute a controlled biodistribution/PK/PD bridging package (rodent plus a large species, preferably NHP) that includes intact‑EV quantitative analytics with vehicle, free‑label, and disrupted‑EV controls, predefined acceptance criteria for CNS exposure and non-vesicular signal, and basic safety/tolerability. Require validated analytics that distinguish intact EV signal from label artifacts and demonstrate PK→PD linkage in the large species before advancement. Major therapeutic advancement decisions require human approval and should remain pending.

flagshipProgram.name: SGL-001
flagshipProgram.subtitle: Flagship therapeutic program of Signal Intelligence · Neuroregeneration and cognitive function
flagshipProgram.oneLineThesis: Product hypothesis: Intranasal mesenchymal-stromal-cell-derived small-EV preparation with defined identity, purity, dose, and a mechanism-relevant potency assay; therapeutic cargo remains to be selected.

thesis.biology: Rodent intranasal MSC-derived EVs show reproducible benefit in injury models and justify further candidate-defining and translational studies but do not by themselves demonstrate intact-EV CNS exposure in larger species.
thesis.product_hypothesis: Intranasal mesenchymal-stromal-cell-derived small-EV preparation with defined identity, purity, dose, and a mechanism-relevant potency assay; therapeutic cargo remains to be selected.
thesis.development_hypothesis: Advancing an intranasal formulation into high-confidence delivery and cross-species PK/PD testing requires completion of a defined CMC/analytics/formulation compatibility gating package.
thesis.development_question: What minimum source-cell, EV identity, cargo, and release definition is required before SGL-001 can be treated as a candidate-like product?

flagshipProgram.currentDetermination: The proposed state change was not sufficiently evidence-supported. No scientific, program, or decision state was changed.
flagshipProgram.strongestCaseFor: No proposed scientific-state update was accepted as sufficiently evidence-supported.
flagshipProgram.strongestCaseAgainst: The reviewer conclusions rely on MISEV2023 as a consensus standard but lack any program-specific experimental/CMC/assay/batch data; therefore the core assertion that SGL-001 meets (or is ready to meet) the specified MCB/WCB, validated intact‑EV assays, stability‑indicating potency, and reproducible GMP‑like production criteria is unproven and remains an unsupported inference from guidance rather than demonstrated fact.
currentBlockers: Cross-species translation uncertainty for intranasal intact-EV CNS exposure
Insufficient CMC/analytics to establish intact-EV identity, potency, and lot-to-lot reproducibility
Model generalizability from injury models to cognition/aging endpoints

developmentGates.name: Product Definition
developmentGates.why_it_matters: What minimum source-cell, EV identity, cargo, and release definition is required before SGL-001 can be treated as a candidate-like product?
what_is_known: Intranasal mesenchymal-stromal-cell-derived small-EV preparation with defined identity, purity, dose, and a mechanism-relevant potency assay; therapeutic cargo remains to be selected.

Rodent intranasal MSC-derived EVs show reproducible benefit in injury models and justify further candidate-defining and translational studies but do not by themselves demonstrate intact-EV CNS exposure in larger species.
what_is_missing: Current materials do not demonstrate characterized source-cell MCB/WCB or scalable, reproducible production sufficient to support advancing a specific intranasal formulation.
developmentGates.next_action: Initiate the two-stage gate: (A) finalize source-cell, create MCB/WCB, define orthogonal QC panel and draft release specs, perform small-scale process dev; (B) run biodistribution/PK/PD bridging study in rodents and a large species (preferably NHP) with vehicle, free-label, and disrupted-EV controls and prespecified acceptance criteria.

developmentGates.name: Potency / Identity
developmentGates.why_it_matters: Lack of MCB/WCB, orthogonal QC, validated potency/stability assays, and scale-up reproducibility may produce misleading in vitro and in vivo results and block regulatory acceptance.
what_is_known: An orthogonal QC panel (particles, protein, lipid markers per MISEV), validated intact-EV assays (LLOQ, specificity, precision), and stability-indicating, mechanism-linked potency assays are required before formulation advancement.
what_is_missing: Lack of MCB/WCB, orthogonal QC, validated potency/stability assays, and scale-up reproducibility may produce misleading in vitro and in vivo results and block regulatory acceptance.
developmentGates.next_action: Identify and cite supporting canonical evidence, or request evidence acquisition; withdraw unsupported conclusions and revisit this matter before proposing a state change.

developmentGates.name: Intranasal Delivery
developmentGates.why_it_matters: Rodent intranasal biodistribution may not predict large-species/NHP CNS exposure for intact EV; device and formulation interactions may differ by species.
what_is_known: Rodent intranasal biodistribution data alone are insufficient to predict reproducible intact-EV CNS exposure in larger species without matching intact-EV assays and bridging controls.
what_is_missing: Rodent intranasal biodistribution may not predict large-species/NHP CNS exposure for intact EV; device and formulation interactions may differ by species.
Current materials do not demonstrate characterized source-cell MCB/WCB or scalable, reproducible production sufficient to support advancing a specific intranasal formulation.
developmentGates.next_action: Require ex vivo nasal recovery and rodent intact-EV-specific PK with controls prior to any large-species study; predefine bridging acceptance criteria and include disrupted-EV and free-label controls in all in vivo studies.

developmentGates.name: Mechanism / Active Biology
developmentGates.why_it_matters: What minimum source-cell, EV identity, cargo, and release definition is required before SGL-001 can be treated as a candidate-like product?
what_is_known: An orthogonal QC panel (particles, protein, lipid markers per MISEV), validated intact-EV assays (LLOQ, specificity, precision), and stability-indicating, mechanism-linked potency assays are required before formulation advancement.
what_is_missing: Intranasal mesenchymal-stromal-cell-derived small-EV preparation with defined identity, purity, dose, and a mechanism-relevant potency assay; therapeutic cargo remains to be selected.
developmentGates.next_action: Initiate the two-stage gate: (A) finalize source-cell, create MCB/WCB, define orthogonal QC panel and draft release specs, perform small-scale process dev; (B) run biodistribution/PK/PD bridging study in rodents and a large species (preferably NHP) with vehicle, free-label, and disrupted-EV controls and prespecified acceptance criteria.

developmentGates.why_it_matters: Efficacy evidence is from acute/injury rodent models; relevance to cognition/aging indications is unproven.
what_is_known: Rodent intranasal MSC-derived EVs show reproducible benefit in injury models and justify further candidate-defining and translational studies but do not by themselves demonstrate intact-EV CNS exposure in larger species.
what_is_missing: Efficacy evidence is from acute/injury rodent models; relevance to cognition/aging indications is unproven.
developmentGates.next_action: Defer indication-specific efficacy studies until biodistribution/PD linkage is demonstrated; design follow-on efficacy models that reflect intended clinical endpoints.

manufacturing.primaryCmcBlocker: Insufficient CMC/analytics to establish intact-EV identity, potency, and lot-to-lot reproducibility
manufacturing.nextManufacturingAction: Define source-cell qualification and MCB/WCB strategy.

cargo.rankingMethodology: Operator focus records the chosen development direction separately from evidence rank. Evidence rank reflects relevance and directness within the current local evidence only; it is not a validated efficacy score and does not override operator choice.

candidates.name: Native MSC-EV secretome cargo
candidates.source: MSC-derived small extracellular vesicles; final source-cell strategy not selected
candidates.mechanism: Multi-component paracrine signaling intended to support neuroregeneration-relevant and inflammation-modulating activity; active components remain undefined.
candidates.rationale: This is the operator-selected program focus because it preserves the multi-component EV thesis and has relevant rodent activity, while MISEV2023 highlights the characterization burden.
candidates.uncertainty: The active cargo components, potency mechanism, source-cell dependence, and relevance to cognition or aging are not established.

candidates.name: Curcumin-loaded EV benchmark
candidates.source: Exogenous curcumin loaded into an exosome preparation
candidates.mechanism: Delivery of an anti-inflammatory small-molecule payload using EVs as a carrier.
candidates.rationale: The current evidence is more cargo-specific than for the native secretome, making this an informative benchmark rather than the selected product focus.
candidates.uncertainty: The cited mouse models and loaded payload do not establish relevance to an unengineered SGL-001 product or human cognitive benefit.

candidates.name: STAT3-inhibitor-loaded EV benchmark
candidates.source: Exogenous STAT3 inhibitor loaded into an exosome preparation
candidates.mechanism: EV-mediated delivery of a pathway-directed inhibitor in a model-specific CNS context.
candidates.rationale: This is retained as a pathway-directed delivery benchmark, not as the current SGL-001 development focus.
candidates.uncertainty: Model-specific activity, payload safety, and relevance to cognition or aging remain unresolved.

candidates.name: miR-21
candidates.mechanism: Anti-apoptotic, pro-angiogenic, pro-survival — the single most consistently reported MSC-EV miRNA across regenerative contexts.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Among the most abundant miRNAs in MSC-EV cargo generally, not a marker specific to regenerative signaling — an 'enrichment' claim needs a naive-EV or non-MSC-EV control to mean anything.
candidates.sourceCitation: Zhu et al., 2017, J Cell Mol Med (MSC-EV miR-21, PTEN/PI3K-Akt cardioprotection)

candidates.name: miR-126
candidates.mechanism: Pro-angiogenic, supports endothelial barrier integrity.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Foundational mechanistic work (Fish et al.) is endothelial-cell biology, not MSC-EV-specific — the MSC-EV cargo literature builds on it rather than originating it.
candidates.sourceCitation: Fish et al., 2008, Dev Cell (foundational, non-MSC); Tao et al., 2017, Theranostics (BMSC-exosome miR-126-3p, diabetic wound)

candidates.name: miR-132
candidates.mechanism: Pro-angiogenic; also reported for neurite outgrowth in CNS contexts.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: RASA1 is a RasGAP acting on Ras/MAPK signaling, not strictly the PI3K-Akt axis — grouped here with the closest recurring node, not a clean fit.
candidates.sourceCitation: Katare et al., 2014, Circ Res (stem-cell-derived exosomal miR-132, cardiac angiogenesis)

candidates.name: miR-146a
candidates.mechanism: Canonically anti-inflammatory via NF-κB dampening, but direction of net effect on inflammation and downstream tissue outcome varies by model and dose.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Reversal is dose- and context-dependent — the same miR-146a delivery has been reported anti-inflammatory in some macrophage/inflammation models and associated with different, sometimes opposing, downstream effects in others. Do not treat 'anti-inflammatory' as a fixed label for this miRNA without checking the specific model.
candidates.sourceCitation: Multiple independent reports of direction-of-effect divergence; representative primary sources need direct verification before citing a specific reversal claim externally.

candidates.name: miR-125b
candidates.mechanism: Regulates apoptosis and proliferation via p53 pathway components; reported both pro-survival (protective, anti-apoptotic) and growth-suppressive depending on target-cell context.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: One of the clearer documented direction-of-effect reversals in this cargo set — p53-axis regulation by miR-125b is well known in the oncology literature to flip between tumor-suppressive and oncogenic roles depending on cell type, and MSC-EV regenerative contexts inherit that same ambiguity rather than resolving it.
candidates.sourceCitation: p53/BAK1 targeting is well established generally; the specific MSC-EV regenerative-context reversal citations need direct verification before external use.

candidates.name: miR-29
candidates.mechanism: Anti-fibrotic — suppresses collagen deposition and extracellular-matrix accumulation; the clearest TGF-β/SMAD-axis counterweight in this cargo set.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Foundational target validation (van Rooij et al.) is direct cardiac-tissue miRNA biology, not MSC-EV cargo transfer specifically — treat as the mechanistic basis the MSC-EV literature draws on.
candidates.sourceCitation: van Rooij et al., 2008, PNAS (miR-29 and cardiac fibrosis via collagen targeting — foundational, non-MSC)

candidates.name: let-7
candidates.mechanism: Differentiation-promoting, anti-proliferative tumor-suppressor family; regulates the stemness-to-senescence transition broadly across tissues.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Family-level entry covering multiple mature let-7 isoforms with overlapping but not identical targets. The documented direction-of-effect reversal is specific to the let-7b isoform (pro- vs. anti-angiogenic reported in different studies) — do not assume it generalizes to the whole family.
candidates.sourceCitation: Roush & Slack, 2008, Trends Cell Biol (let-7 family review, foundational, non-MSC); let-7b-specific reversal citations need direct verification.

candidates.name: miR-210
candidates.mechanism: The archetypal 'hypoxamir' — induced under hypoxic preconditioning, pro-angiogenic and pro-survival under ischemic conditions.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Effect and abundance are strongly dependent on whether the parental MSCs were hypoxia-preconditioned before EV harvest — normoxic-culture MSC-EVs carry substantially less miR-210, and results don't transfer across culture conditions.
candidates.sourceCitation: Chan & Loscalzo, 2010, Cell Cycle (miR-210 as 'hypoxamir', foundational review, non-MSC-specific)

candidates.name: miR-221/222
candidates.mechanism: Promotes proliferation and reduces apoptosis via p27/p57 suppression; also reported to modulate angiogenesis.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Foundational target-validation work is oncology-derived (proliferation control), not MSC-EV-specific — the regenerative-context application is a later extension.
candidates.sourceCitation: le Sage et al., 2007, EMBO J (miR-221/222 regulation of p27Kip1 — foundational, non-MSC)

candidates.name: miR-133b
candidates.mechanism: Promotes neurite outgrowth and neural plasticity; anti-fibrotic via CTGF suppression.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: The strongest single MSC-EV in-vivo functional-transfer demonstration in this cargo set (rat stroke model, direct EV-mediated transfer shown), which is why it's a common reference point in the stoichiometry debate about whether EV miRNA cargo can be functionally meaningful at reported copy numbers.
candidates.sourceCitation: Xin et al., 2013, Stem Cells (MSC-exosome miR-133b transfer, neural plasticity and functional recovery after stroke in rats)

candidates.name: miR-17-92
candidates.mechanism: Cluster-level pro-angiogenic and pro-neurogenic effect via suppression of anti-angiogenic targets (CTGF, TSP1) alongside direct PTEN suppression.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Cluster of six co-transcribed miRNAs (17, 18a, 19a, 19b, 20a, 92a) reported as a unit in most MSC-EV work — individual-member contributions are not always separated. The documented direction-of-effect reversal in this cargo set is specific to the miR-92a member, not the cluster as a whole.
candidates.sourceCitation: Xin et al., 2017, Stem Cells (MSC-exosome miR-17-92 cluster enrichment, neuroplasticity and functional recovery after stroke in rats)

candidates.name: miR-486-5p
candidates.mechanism: Muscle-enriched miRNA; promotes myoblast survival/regeneration and is separately reported cardioprotective via the same PTEN axis.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Foundational work establishes this as a muscle-tissue-intrinsic miRNA (myomiR), not an MSC-EV discovery — MSC-EV cargo studies build on that baseline biology.
candidates.sourceCitation: Small et al., 2010, PNAS (miR-486 regulation of PI3K/Akt signaling via PTEN, muscle-enriched — foundational, non-MSC)

candidates.name: miR-22-3p
candidates.mechanism: Anti-apoptotic and anti-fibrotic in cardiac contexts, reported to act partly through HMGB1-mediated inflammatory signaling suppression.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Lower citation confidence than most entries in this file — the foundational cardiac-hypertrophy role of miR-22 is well established, but the specific MSC-EV cargo delivery mechanism is a thinner literature and needs direct verification before use.
candidates.sourceCitation: Huang et al., 2013, Circ Res (miR-22 and cardiac hypertrophy — foundational, non-MSC-EV-specific; MSC-EV-specific citation not confidently recalled)

candidates.name: miR-100-5p
candidates.mechanism: Induces autophagy via mTOR suppression; reported neuroprotective and (separately, in tumor angiogenesis literature) anti-angiogenic depending on context.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: The anti-angiogenic mTOR-suppression literature for this miRNA is largely tumor-biology work, not regenerative-medicine work — the neuroprotective/autophagy framing used here is the regenerative-context reading, and the two literatures shouldn't be conflated.
candidates.sourceCitation: Grundmann et al., 2011, Circulation (miR-100 regulation of neovascularization via mTOR suppression — foundational, non-MSC-EV-specific)

candidates.name: miR-181
candidates.mechanism: Family-level entry (181a/b/c/d) — reported roles in myogenesis, immune modulation, and (miR-181c specifically) mitochondrial gene regulation.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Family members have distinct, sometimes non-overlapping target sets — treating 'miR-181' as one biological entity for scoring purposes understates real isoform-level heterogeneity. Isoform should be specified before any claim is used downstream of this record.
candidates.sourceCitation: Indrieri et al., 2020, EMBO Mol Med (miR-181a/b and mitochondrial disease models — moderate citation confidence, verify directly)

candidates.name: miR-24
candidates.mechanism: Anti-apoptotic cardioprotection via Bim suppression.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Engineered/loaded cargo — enriched via parental-cell genetic modification (GATA-4 overexpression), not representative of naive MSC-EV content. Per the literature agent's standing rule, findings here do not transfer to an unloaded/naive product without separate confirmation.
candidates.sourceCitation: Yu et al., 2015, Int J Cardiol (GATA-4-overexpressing MSC exosomes as a reservoir of anti-apoptotic miRNAs, cardioprotection)

candidates.name: miR-19a
candidates.mechanism: Anti-apoptotic and anti-inflammatory (macrophage polarization) cardioprotection; co-reported alongside miR-24 in the same engineered-cargo model.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Engineered/loaded cargo — same GATA-4-overexpression construct as miR-24 above. Also a native member of the miR-17-92 cluster (see that entry) — the engineered version here is deliberately enriched beyond native cluster levels, so this is not simply 'more of the same cargo.'
candidates.sourceCitation: Yu et al., 2015, Int J Cardiol (GATA-4-overexpressing MSC exosomes, miR-19a, PTEN/SOCS1, cardioprotection)

candidates.name: miR-410
candidates.mechanism: Chondroprotective, anti-catabolic in osteoarthritis models — reported to suppress Wnt-pathway-driven cartilage degradation.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Engineered/loaded cargo, and this is the lowest-confidence citation in the file — the target/pathway assignment is directionally consistent with the broader engineered-MSC-EV cartilage literature but the specific primary paper was not confidently recalled. Verify before relying on this entry for anything beyond a placeholder.
candidates.sourceCitation: Not confidently recalled — requires a direct literature search before citing; tentatively associated with engineered MSC-EV osteoarthritis chondroprotection studies.

candidates.name: miR-214-3p
candidates.mechanism: Native miR-214-3p (notably from osteoclast-derived EVs) suppresses osteoblastic bone formation via ATF4; the engineered regenerative application uses an anti-miR-214-3p construct loaded into MSC-EVs to counteract that suppression and promote osteogenesis.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'msc'.
candidates.uncertainty: Direction of effect depends entirely on whether the cargo is native miR-214-3p (bone-formation-suppressive, originally characterized in osteoclast-derived EVs, not MSC-EVs) or an engineered anti-miR-214-3p construct (bone-formation-promoting). These are opposite interventions sharing one entry — do not read 'effect' without checking which construct a given source used.
candidates.sourceCitation: Sun et al., 2016, J Extracell Vesicles / Bone Research (osteoclast-derived exosomal miR-214-3p inhibits osteoblastic bone formation via ATF4 — the suppressive/native finding this engineered application is designed to counteract)

candidates.name: miR-302
candidates.mechanism: Maintains pluripotency and promotes reprogramming efficiency by driving a rapid G1/S cell-cycle transition characteristic of pluripotent cells.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'pluripotent'.
candidates.uncertainty: The foundational literature is about the miRNA itself (transfection/expression), not EV-mediated transfer — whether ESC/iPSC-EVs carry functionally sufficient miR-302 cargo to reproduce these effects is a separate, less-established question from the direct-expression literature this citation reflects.
candidates.sourceCitation: Judson et al., 2009, Nat Biotechnol (embryonic-stem-cell-specific microRNAs, including the miR-302 cluster, promote induced pluripotency)

candidates.name: miR-371-373
candidates.mechanism: Human-ESC-specific cluster supporting proliferation and pluripotency maintenance via p21 and Hippo-pathway (LATS2) suppression.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'pluripotent'.
candidates.uncertainty: This cluster's largest, best-established literature is oncology (germ-cell-tumor biomarker), not regenerative medicine — the regenerative framing here is a minority use case within the broader miR-371-373 literature and should not be assumed to carry the same weight of evidence.
candidates.sourceCitation: Voorhoeve et al., 2006, Cell (miR-372/373 as oncogenes in testicular germ-cell tumors — the field's dominant citation for this cluster, not a regenerative-medicine paper)

candidates.name: miR-290-295
candidates.mechanism: Drives G1/S transition and self-renewal in mouse ESCs; regulates de novo DNA methylation indirectly via RBL2 suppression of DNMT3A/B.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'pluripotent'.
candidates.uncertainty: Mouse-specific cluster with no direct human ortholog — miR-371-373 is the human-ESC functional analogue, not the same sequence. Do not treat findings here as transferable to human cells without that substitution already made in the source study.
candidates.sourceCitation: Sinkkonen et al., 2008, Nat Struct Mol Biol (miR-290 cluster controls de novo DNA methylation via Rbl2/Dnmt3 in mouse ESCs)

candidates.name: miR-9-5p
candidates.mechanism: Dual/opposing roles reported in neural stem cell fate: represses TLX to promote differentiation while other reported activity supports proliferation — a feedback loop rather than a one-directional effect.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'pluripotent'.
candidates.uncertainty: Not included in this file's explicit context-dependent flag list, but the underlying biology (a feedback loop with opposing arms) is functionally similar to the flagged entries — worth treating with the same caution even though it isn't formally tagged that way here.
candidates.sourceCitation: Zhao, Sun, Li & Shi, 2009, Nat Struct Mol Biol (miR-9/TLX feedback loop in neural stem cell fate determination)

candidates.name: miR-296-5p
candidates.source: endothelial progenitor cells, tumor endothelium (adjacent literature)
candidates.mechanism: Pro-angiogenic — suppresses HGS-mediated degradation of growth factor receptors (VEGFR2, PDGFRβ), increasing their surface availability.
candidates.rationale: Imported biological-design candidate from legacy tier 'pluripotent'.
candidates.uncertainty: Most of the primary literature for this miRNA is tumor-angiogenesis research, not regenerative medicine — included here because the mechanism (angiogenic receptor recycling) is directly relevant to regenerative vascularization, but the source literature's intent was oncology, and that context should travel with any citation of it.
candidates.sourceCitation: Würdinger et al., 2008, Cancer Cell (miR-296 regulates growth-factor-receptor overexpression in angiogenic endothelial cells)

pathways.name: Neuroinflammation modulation
pathways.description: Inflammation-modulating activity reported across local preclinical EV evidence; direction and causal cargo are product- and model-dependent.

pathways.name: Neurogenesis and neural plasticity
pathways.description: Preservation or modulation of neurogenesis and functional outcomes observed in rodent injury models, not established in aging or humans.

theoreticalMoa.title: Theoretical SGL-001 mechanism of action
theoreticalMoa.subtitle: From manufactured cargo to a proposed regenerative tissue response
theoreticalMoa.disclaimer: This is a testable mechanism hypothesis, not an established SGL-001 mechanism. Each transition must be demonstrated experimentally for the final product.

steps.title: Reproducible miRNA cargo
steps.description: A manufactured SGL-001 lot contains a defined and reproducible miRNA signature.
steps.validationGate: Quantify absolute miRNA copies across multiple released lots.

steps.title: Functional EV association
steps.description: Candidate miRNA is protected within functional EVs rather than free, degraded, or co-isolated material.
steps.validationGate: Demonstrate vesicular localization with orthogonal separation and protection assays.

steps.title: Intranasal exposure
steps.description: The formulation remains stable after dosing and reaches a biologically relevant nasal or CNS target compartment.
steps.validationGate: Measure biodistribution and exposure in a relevant large-animal model.

steps.title: Target-cell uptake
steps.description: Relevant recipient cells internalize SGL-001 EVs or their active cargo.
steps.validationGate: Show cell-specific uptake using traceable, artifact-controlled methods.

steps.title: Endosomal escape
steps.description: Internalized miRNA reaches the cytoplasm instead of remaining trapped or being degraded.
steps.validationGate: Demonstrate cytosolic delivery and functional accessibility.

steps.title: RISC engagement at sufficient dose
steps.description: Delivered miRNA loads into Argonaute/RISC at a concentration capable of regulating gene expression.
steps.evidenceStatus: Established general biology; unconfirmed for SGL-001
steps.validationGate: Measure Ago loading, intracellular copy number, and dose-response.

steps.title: Direct target repression
steps.description: The engaged miRNA reduces a defined target mRNA or protein, such as a pathway inhibitor.
steps.validationGate: Confirm direct target engagement and rescue the effect by blocking the miRNA.

steps.title: Pathway modulation
steps.description: Target repression changes a relevant signaling system such as PTEN/PI3K-AKT, NF-kB, or TGF-beta/SMAD.
steps.validationGate: Measure pathway direction, magnitude, timing, and cell specificity.

steps.title: Regenerative tissue response
steps.description: Pathway changes produce a reproducible phenotype such as neural plasticity, inflammatory resolution, or tissue repair.
steps.validationGate: Link the phenotype causally to cargo, target, and pathway using loss-of-function controls.

theoreticalMoa.conclusion: SGL-001 currently has a proposed multi-component paracrine mechanism. No specific miRNA, target, pathway, or clinical effect has yet been established as its mechanism of action.

excipients.name: Monobasic potassium phosphate / dibasic sodium phosphate
excipients.risk: 10 mM stays well below the ~0.13 M threshold where a buffer starts overriding nasal pH (Washington et al. 2000), but the molarity itself is transferred from a lyophilisate study, not derived for this product.
excipients.precedentSummary: IID nasal MONOBASIC POTASSIUM PHOSPHATE; TOSYMRA (NDA 210884); SPRIX (NDA 022382)
excipients.tradeoff: 10 mM stays well below the ~0.13 M threshold where a buffer starts overriding nasal pH (Washington et al. 2000), but the molarity itself is transferred from a lyophilisate study, not derived for this product.

excipients.name: Sodium chloride
excipients.risk: Level is open pending the stabilizer decision, since the stabilizer itself contributes osmolality; counter-ion identity (Na⁺ vs K⁺) may matter more to vesicle stability than a tonicity calculation captures.
excipients.precedentSummary: IID nasal SOLUTION 330 mg / LIQUID 7.4 mg/mL; TOSYMRA; calcitonin-salmon nasal spray
excipients.tradeoff: Level is open pending the stabilizer decision, since the stabilizer itself contributes osmolality; counter-ion identity (Na⁺ vs K⁺) may matter more to vesicle stability than a tonicity calculation captures.

excipients.name: Trehalose (25 mM)
excipients.risk: Deepest EV-specific stabilization evidence of any excipient considered (Bosch 2016, Görgens 2022, Charoenviriyakul 2018), but would need a nasal-route safety qualification package.
excipients.precedentSummary: no precedent — regulatory risk (IID: intradermal, subcutaneous only; no nasal-route entry)
excipients.tradeoff: Deepest EV-specific stabilization evidence of any excipient considered (Bosch 2016, Görgens 2022, Charoenviriyakul 2018), but would need a nasal-route safety qualification package.

excipients.name: Mannitol
excipients.risk: Only sugar/polyol with nasal precedent and a stated max potency, but a crystallizing bulking agent — a weaker lyoprotectant for a membrane particle than an amorphous disaccharide; no EV-specific data found.
excipients.tradeoff: Only sugar/polyol with nasal precedent and a stated max potency, but a crystallizing bulking agent — a weaker lyoprotectant for a membrane particle than an amorphous disaccharide; no EV-specific data found.

excipients.name: Human serum albumin (0.2%)
excipients.risk: Suppresses the plastic-surface EV adsorption loss Görgens (2022) measured within minutes, but carries no nasal-route precedent at all.
excipients.precedentSummary: no precedent — regulatory risk (IID: intravenous, oral only; no nasal-route entry)
excipients.tradeoff: Suppresses the plastic-surface EV adsorption loss Görgens (2022) measured within minutes, but carries no nasal-route precedent at all.

excipients.name: HEPES (25 mM)
excipients.risk: Buffer base of PBS-HAT, the lead published EV-stabilization buffer (Görgens 2022), but has no US excipient precedent whatsoever.
excipients.precedentSummary: no precedent — regulatory risk (absent from the IID entirely, by any route)
excipients.tradeoff: Buffer base of PBS-HAT, the lead published EV-stabilization buffer (Görgens 2022), but has no US excipient precedent whatsoever.

excipients.name: Sucrose (5%)
excipients.risk: Improves EV colloidal stability on freeze-thaw and supports a lyophilisate stable 6 months at 40°C (Trenkenschuh 2022), but zero nasal-route precedent.
excipients.precedentSummary: no precedent — regulatory risk (IID: 10 other routes incl. IV, ophthalmic, oral; no nasal-route entry)
excipients.tradeoff: Improves EV colloidal stability on freeze-thaw and supports a lyophilisate stable 6 months at 40°C (Trenkenschuh 2022), but zero nasal-route precedent.

excipients.name: Poloxamer 188 (0.02%)
excipients.risk: The single most effective published EV colloidal-stability agent (Trenkenschuh 2022), but zero nasal-route precedent.
excipients.precedentSummary: no precedent — regulatory risk (IID: 7 other routes incl. IV, ophthalmic, intratympanic; no nasal-route entry)
excipients.tradeoff: The single most effective published EV colloidal-stability agent (Trenkenschuh 2022), but zero nasal-route precedent.

excipients.name: Polysorbate 80 (0.01% w/v)
excipients.risk: The nasal-precedented stand-in for poloxamer 188, but its CMC is in the low micromolar range — even 0.01% sits above it, the same surfactant-above-CMC property that disqualified DDM, unmeasured against these vesicles.
excipients.precedentSummary: IID nasal SPRAY, METERED, 0.1 mg/1 mL
excipients.tradeoff: The nasal-precedented stand-in for poloxamer 188, but its CMC is in the low micromolar range — even 0.01% sits above it, the same surfactant-above-CMC property that disqualified DDM, unmeasured against these vesicles.

excipients.name: Hypromellose 2910 (5 mPa·s)
excipients.risk: Deliberately deferred, not chosen: added viscosity coarsens the plume and risks the <4.6% olfactory deposition fraction the product depends on; cellulose-polymer/EV adsorption compatibility is untested.
excipients.precedentSummary: IID nasal SPRAY/SPRAY METERED, 1 mg/1 mL; seen in azelastine ANDAs
excipients.tradeoff: Deliberately deferred, not chosen: added viscosity coarsens the plume and risks the <4.6% olfactory deposition fraction the product depends on; cellulose-polymer/EV adsorption compatibility is untested.

excipients.name: n-Dodecyl β-D-maltoside (DDM / Intravail)
excipients.risk: ~23× its own CMC and roughly 500 mol detergent per mol lipid at this product's target particle concentration — would be expected to dissolve the vesicle active.
excipients.precedentSummary: IID nasal SPRAY; TOSYMRA (NDA 210884) at 0.2% w/v
excipients.tradeoff: ~23× its own CMC and roughly 500 mol detergent per mol lipid at this product's target particle concentration — would be expected to dissolve the vesicle active.

excipients.name: Chitosan
excipients.risk: Frequently proposed in the delivery literature as a nasal permeation enhancer, but its cationic, membrane-interacting mode of action raises the same vesicle-disruption question as every other enhancer here.
excipients.precedentSummary: no precedent — regulatory risk (absent from the nasal IID and from all 694 nasal labels)
excipients.tradeoff: Frequently proposed in the delivery literature as a nasal permeation enhancer, but its cationic, membrane-interacting mode of action raises the same vesicle-disruption question as every other enhancer here.

excipients.name: Benzalkonium chloride (BAC)
excipients.risk: Ciliotoxic at nasal use concentrations (Riechelmann et al. 2004, p<0.0001); a cationic surfactant in continuous contact with a vesicle active for the whole in-use life of the bottle.
excipients.precedentSummary: the dominant nasal preservative, 535 of 694 nasal labels
excipients.tradeoff: Ciliotoxic at nasal use concentrations (Riechelmann et al. 2004, p<0.0001); a cationic surfactant in continuous contact with a vesicle active for the whole in-use life of the bottle.

excipients.name: Plain PBS (as vehicle)
excipients.risk: Severe EV recovery loss within days on storage and within minutes on dilution (Görgens et al. 2022); ranked below potassium phosphate for EV stability (Trenkenschuh et al. 2022).
excipients.precedentSummary: sodium chloride and sodium phosphate both have nasal precedent
excipients.tradeoff: Severe EV recovery loss within days on storage and within minutes on dilution (Görgens et al. 2022); ranked below potassium phosphate for EV stability (Trenkenschuh et al. 2022).

excipients.name: Citrate buffer
excipients.risk: Good nasal precedent, but buffers to pH 5–6 — the acidic region associated with EV aggregation and vesicle fusion (Trenkenschuh et al. 2022). Precedent for the wrong pH.
excipients.precedentSummary: IID nasal citrate entries; TOSYMRA uses citric acid monohydrate
excipients.tradeoff: Good nasal precedent, but buffers to pH 5–6 — the acidic region associated with EV aggregation and vesicle fusion (Trenkenschuh et al. 2022). Precedent for the wrong pH.

presentations.shelfLife: unpublished by Signal; site meta description claims "shelf-stable" but no storage temperature or duration appears anywhere on the page (fetched 2026-09-03)
presentations.userSteps: single actuation from a 10 mL multi-dose metered spray, no reconstitution
presentations.verdict: unsupported as currently specified — EVs in aqueous buffer without a nasal-precedented stabilizer lose recoverable particles within minutes to days (Görgens et al. 2022); the "shelf-stable" claim has no formulation or storage-condition evidence behind it.

presentations.shelfLife: 6 months at 40°C for particle size and concentration (Trenkenschuh et al. 2022) — the only published route to anything resembling "shelf-stable" for this active; not tested for this specific formulation
presentations.coldChain: not required for storage per the cited lyophilisate data; unconfirmed for this product
presentations.userSteps: reconstitute the lyophilized cake with diluent before use, then spray — an added step versus the currently marketed single-actuation format
presentations.verdict: best-evidenced route to a genuine stability claim, but presentation-and-device.md (device, fill, reconstitution spec) does not exist yet, and it changes the stabilizer decision from a cryoprotectant-in-solution to a lyophilisate cake.

presentations.shelfLife: consensus long-term storage condition for EV preparations at −80°C (Ahmadian et al. 2024, cited via sgl-001-spec.md); one freeze-thaw cycle costs 23–36% of particles
presentations.coldChain: required — an unbroken −80°C freezer chain from manufacture through point of use
presentations.userSteps: thaw before each use; repeated freeze-thaw is destructive, so single-use aliquots would be needed rather than a multi-dose bottle
presentations.verdict: ruled out for a consumer multi-dose product — the cold-chain requirement and per-cycle particle loss are incompatible with a bottle used over multiple days and with the site's own "shelf-stable" framing.

jurisdictions.productClassification: SB 1768's HCT/P definition excludes secreted and extracted human products and cell factors, and requires viable live cells on post-thaw analysis (Fla. Stat. §458.3245(2)(a)3., §458.3245(3)(b)3.). Federally, FDA treats unapproved exosome products as outside HCT/P status and unlawful when marketed with therapeutic claims — the state pathway does not reach this product, and a state law cannot authorise what federal law prohibits.
jurisdictions.privateClinicPath: FL-licensed MD/DO physicians may perform non-FDA-approved stem cell therapy, but only for orthopedics, wound care, and pain management, with informed consent and an advertising notice (Fla. Stat. §458.3245, effective 2025-07-01). Route note: Not a route for exosomes. Watch whether Georgia HB 1275 and Tennessee HB 2246, both signed May 2026, use definitions including cell-derived products.
jurisdictions.conciseRationale: This is the shape the category's near future may take elsewhere: a state creates a real, permissive pathway for a cellular therapy, a commercial market reads it as covering more than it does, and federal enforcement escalates against that gap. Florida is where that pattern is furthest along and most visible right now.

jurisdictions.productClassification: No product-specific classification for exosomes or secretome exists. A cell-free biologic would most plausibly need COFEPRIS sanitary registration as a 'medicamento biotecnológico' (Art. 222 Bis, Ley General de Salud), but Mexico's dedicated regenerative-medicine framework (Art. 315 licensing; the January 2026 LGS reform's definitions, consent, and anti-commerce rules) is built entirely around 'células troncales' (living stem cells) — exosomes, extracellular vesicles, and secretome are not mentioned anywhere in that reform's text, fetched and searched in full this run.
jurisdictions.privateClinicPath: COFEPRIS-authorized regenerative-medicine establishments and stem cell banks/collection centers may administer stem cell therapy under Art. 315 licensing and the 2026 reform's committee and consent requirements. Whether an acellular exosome/secretome product is administered under that same authorization in practice, or falls outside it, is unresolved — clinic-marketing sources describe exosome therapy being offered under the same facility authorization as stem cell therapy, with no regulatory differentiation found. Route note: Mexico already has an active, internationally-marketed private clinic sector for stem cell and exosome therapy, operating on facility-level COFEPRIS authorization (Aviso de Funcionamiento, Aviso de Publicidad) rather than product-level drug registration, per clinic-operator sources. The fast route mirrors that practice; the durable route is COFEPRIS product registration as a medicamento biotecnológico (Art. 222 Bis) — or asking COFEPRIS directly whether the 2026 stem-cell-establishment framework reaches an acellular product.
jurisdictions.conciseRationale: Mexico already has an active, internationally-marketed private clinic sector for stem cell and exosome therapy, operating on facility-level COFEPRIS authorization (Aviso de Funcionamiento, Aviso de Publicidad) rather than product-level drug registration, per clinic-operator sources. The fast route mirrors that practice; the durable route is COFEPRIS product registration as a medicamento biotecnológico (Art. 222 Bis) — or asking COFEPRIS directly whether the 2026 stem-cell-establishment framework reaches an acellular product.
unresolvedQuestions: Whether COFEPRIS or a court has ever addressed whether the 2026 stem-cell reform's definitions extend to an acellular exosome/secretome product — no primary source found either way

Whether Mexican private clinics selling exosome/secretome therapy in practice hold a registro sanitario under Art. 222 Bis, or operate solely under facility/advertising notices — described one way by clinic-operator sources, not independently confirmed against a COFEPRIS registry

Whether the widely-repeated media claim that the 2026 reform specifically names adipose tissue, placental tissue, dental pulp, and umbilical cord as 'mesenchymal progenitor cell' sources is accurate — the full decree text (fetched and searched in full this run) does not contain the word 'mesenquimal' anywhere, only the generic term 'células troncales'; this discrepancy between secondary reporting and the primary text is unresolved
No specific COFEPRIS enforcement action against an exosome or regenerative-medicine clinic was found this run — a negative search result, not evidence of absence

designLab.disclaimer: AI-generated, evidence-linked product hypotheses. These are not validated mechanisms, manufacturing specifications, experimental results, or evidence of clinical efficacy.
designLab.currentDesignQuestion: Daily question: After passage through the candidate intranasal device and exposure to candidate formulation buffers, can a spike-in–controlled, multi-epitope intact-EV surface-phenotype workflow (multi-epitope immuno-capture on intact material + particle-peak co-localization + detergent/protease sensitivity) reproducibly discriminate EV-enriched bounded fractions from secretome-retaining concentrates as a product-identity metric (non-potency)?

latestReviewedHypothesis.title: Hypothesis: A spike-in–controlled, multi-epitope intact-EV surface-phenotype assay preserved after device/formulation passage discriminates an EV-enriched bounded fraction from secretome and provides a non-potency product-identity gate for SGL-001
latestReviewedHypothesis.designQuestion: Daily question: After passage through the candidate intranasal device and exposure to candidate formulation buffers, can a spike-in–controlled, multi-epitope intact-EV surface-phenotype workflow (multi-epitope immuno-capture on intact material + particle-peak co-localization + detergent/protease sensitivity) reproducibly discriminate EV-enriched bounded fractions from secretome-retaining concentrates as a product-identity metric (non-potency)?
latestReviewedHypothesis.proposedProductChangeOrAttribute: Adopt a spike-in–controlled surface-phenotype identity gate: multi-epitope capture-positive signal (CD63/CD9/CD81 ± TIM4/AnxA5) on intact material that (A) co-localizes with particle-count peaks in density/size-bounded fractions after realistic device/formulation passage, and (B) is substantially reduced or abolished after detergent + protease/RNase treatment (detergent sensitivity). Use preservation of this composite surface-phenotype as a qualitative pass/fail identity gate (non-numeric) to classify a preparation as an EV-enriched bounded drug-substance candidate for downstream CMC and comparability workflows.
latestReviewedHypothesis.biologicalRationale: MISEV2023 and program preclinical literature emphasize that canonical marker signal can arise from non-vesicular co-isolates; combining intact immuno-capture with particle-peak co-localization and membrane-protection tests (and controlling for assay recovery with an exogenous intact-EV spike-in) is the minimal orthogonal approach to distinguish bona fide membrane-protected EV surface phenotype from soluble/aggregate confounders, and to determine whether device/formulation passage preserves identity-relevant epitopes needed for intranasal deployment.
latestReviewedHypothesis.manufacturingRationale: A spike-in–validated intact-surface-phenotype gate provides a qualitative, actionable identity metric that can be applied after formulation and device compatibility testing and after scale-relevant concentration steps; it supports go/no-go comparability and avoids premature numeric spec setting until multi-site reproducibility and assay validation are demonstrated.
latestReviewedHypothesis.expectedMeasurableEffect: Qualitative pass/fail identity calls per condition: 'EV-enriched pass' if (A) exogenous intact-EV spike-in is recovered and membrane-protected in capture-positive particle-peak fractions, (B) endogenous multi-epitope capture signal co-localizes with particle-count peaks after device/formulation passage, and (C) capture signal is abolished or substantially reduced after detergent + protease/RNase; otherwise 'fail' (treated as secretome-like).

nodes.statement: If an EV-enriched bounded fraction displays multi-epitope immuno-capture signal on intact material that co-localizes with particle-count peaks and is lost after detergent + protease/RNase, then that signal reports membrane-protected EV surface phenotype distinguishable from soluble secretome co-isolates.

If the multi-epitope, spike-in–validated surface-phenotype is preserved after passage through the intended nasal device and candidate formulation buffers, then the preparation retains an operational identity attribute compatible with intranasal delivery and downstream CMC comparability.

If the surface-phenotype is lost after device/formulation passage (despite spike-in recovery), then observed marker signal reflects assay or secretome artifacts and the material should not be advanced as an EV-enriched drug-substance for intranasal use.

edges.uncertainty: Moderate: MISEV supports orthogonal approaches; large-animal intranasal negative biodistribution motivates testing whether identity survives delivery stresses.
edges.competing_explanation: Preserved capture signal after device/formulation might reflect selective survival of a non-vesicular complex that binds capture reagents and resists detergent/protease in the chosen assay conditions.
edges.missing_experiment: Spike-in–controlled device/formulation passage followed by fraction-level detergent/protease protection to rule out non-vesicular survivor artifacts.

edges.uncertainty: Moderate-to-high: identity preservation is necessary but may not guarantee cross-species recoverability or downstream potency; further in vivo bridging would be required.
edges.competing_explanation: Loss of surface-phenotype after passage could reflect capture-reagent incompatibility with formulation excipients rather than true epitope masking or membrane damage.
edges.missing_experiment: Capture-compatibility panels for each formulation buffer and device rinse to exclude assay interference.

reviewerFindings.conclusion: The proposal is conceptually consistent with and appropriately attributed to the cited canonical evidence (MISEV2023 for need for orthogonal characterization and Driedonks et al. for intranasal translational risk), and the proposal correctly treats the macaque negative-biodistribution data as a limiting/contradicting input rather than positive proof of delivery. However, the specific operational claim that a pre-device spike-in plus intact multi-epitope immuno-capture co-localized with particle peaks and detergent/protease sensitivity will reproducibly distinguish EV-enriched fractions from secretome across formulation/device stresses lacks direct experimental support in the supplied evidence set — MISEV provides methodological recommendations but not direct experimental validation of this exact spike-in + intact-capture workflow, and the macaque study documents delivery limitations but does not validate the proposed analytic gate. Therefore the design is plausible and well-attributed but not fully supported by the provided canonical evidence.
reviewerFindings.evidence_gap: No supplied canonical evidence demonstrates empirical validation of the proposed combined workflow (exogenous intact-EV spike-in applied prior to device/formulation passage + intact multi-epitope immuno-capture co-localized with particle peaks + detergent/protease protection) as an operational discriminator of EV-enriched versus secretome-retaining concentrates. Also absent is evidence that candidate spike-in tracers faithfully mimic endogenous EV behavior across device/formulation stresses and capture assays.
concerns: Primary operational claim lacks direct experimental validation in the cited literature (MISEV is a guideline; Driedonks documents intranasal biodistribution limitations but does not test the analytic gate).

Risk of false positives: non-vesicular complexes that bind capture reagents and resist detergent/protease under the chosen assay conditions could produce misleading 'pass' calls (this competing explanation is noted but not resolved by the provided evidence).

Assay interference: formulation excipients or device rinse residues could mask or mimic capture signal; MISEV recommends controls but does not provide specific compatibility outcomes for the proposed capture panel/formulations.

Spike-in representativeness: no cited evidence here shows that an exogenous intact-EV spike-in will replicate endogenous EV susceptibility to device/formulation stresses and capture-recovery, complicating interpretation of recovery-based controls.

reviewerFindings.conclusion: Supported as a plausible, manufacturable non‑potency identity gate but requires targeted experiments and controls before CMC adoption. The proposed spike‑in–validated intact multi‑epitope capture + particle‑peak co‑localization + detergent/protease protection workflow is implementable with standard analytical platforms (immuno‑capture, fractionation, particle counting), and it addresses key MISEV2023 concerns about co‑isolates and orthogonal characterization. Major residual risks relate to spike‑in sourcing/behavior, assay interference from formulation/device matrices, potential detergent‑resistant non‑vesicular artifacts, lot‑to‑lot reproducibility, and scale/flow stresses not yet bridged to large‑scale manufacture or NHP biodistribution.
reviewerFindings.evidence_gap: No direct experimental evidence is provided that a spike‑in–controlled intact‑capture + fractionation + detergent/protease protection workflow survives the candidate intranasal device/formulation passage across scaled lots; missing are (1) spike‑in behavior/availability data, (2) capture‑compatibility panels for the specific formulation/device matrices, (3) multi‑lot (≥3) reproducibility and inter‑site assay validation, and (4) demonstration that the gate scales without unacceptable particle/protein loss or changes in stability.
concerns: Spike‑in tracer availability and representativeness: choice and validation of an exogenous intact‑EV tracer that mimics endogenous EV behavior across fractionation and device shear is critical and currently unresolved (manufacturing and measurement feasibility risk).

Assay interference and false negatives/positives: formulation excipients or device rinse residues can mask capture epitopes (false loss) or bind capture reagents (false positive); capture‑compatibility panels and buffer controls are required before using the gate for comparability decisions (process sensitivity and measurement feasibility concern).

Detergent/protease resistance of non‑vesicular complexes: some non‑vesicular co‑isolates may resist the planned protection assay under chosen conditions, producing false positives; orthogonal orthogonalization (e.g., alternative membrane‑disruption chemistries or cargo protection readouts) may be needed (measurement feasibility and QA relevance).

Lot comparability and reproducibility: the gate is qualitative and dependent on replicate concordance across ≥3 independent conditioned‑medium lots; without demonstrated cross‑lot reproducibility and inter‑operator/site robustness, the gate cannot reliably support comparability or release decisions (lot comparability risk).

Scale‑up and device shear: passage through clinical device prototypes or scale‑relevant flow rigs may induce epitope loss or particle aggregation not observed at small scale; risk of product loss or altered identity during scale‑up and fill/finish steps (scale‑up and stability risk).

Stability in candidate formulations: compatibility of EV surface phenotype with intended excipient matrix over intended storage/handling conditions is unproven; the gate could fail during stability stress even if initial passage is acceptable (stability risk).

Measurement limits: particle counters and fractionation methods have limits and may not resolve low‑abundance, co‑localized signals post‑device/formulation; sensitivity must be demonstrated to avoid false negatives (measurement feasibility).

Regulatory interpretation: a qualitative pass/fail identity gate is pragmatic pre‑specification, but regulators will expect documented orthogonality, reproducibility, and justification before accepting it as a comparability/identity criterion (QA relevance).

reviewerFindings.conclusion: The proposed spike-in–controlled, multi-epitope intact-EV surface‑phenotype workflow is a causally plausible and appropriate analytical approach to discriminate membrane‑protected, capture‑positive particle fractions from secretome-derived, capture-positive artifacts after device/formulation passage. If executed with the specified orthogonal controls (exogenous intact‑EV spike‑in added before passage, fraction‑level particle-peak co‑localization, detergent+protease/RNase protection, and capture‑compatibility panels), the experiment should meaningfully distinguish the two competing explanations named in the design (true membrane‑protected EVs vs. capture‑binding non‑vesicular survivors or assay interference). However, confidence is moderate rather than high because (1) detergent/protease resistance is an operational test that can give false positives for some non-vesicular complexes and (2) spike‑in tracers may not perfectly mimic endogenous material under device/formulation stresses. The experiment, as proposed, does not and does not claim to establish delivery to brain or potency; those remain separate translational questions requiring in vivo or functional bridging studies.
reviewerFindings.evidence_gap: Key gaps: (A) lack of direct in vivo linkage showing that preservation of the proposed surface‑phenotype after device/formulation passage predicts in‑host biodistribution or functional/therapeutic readouts; (B) limited orthogonal demonstration that detergent+protease resistance in the chosen capture format cannot be exhibited by non‑vesicular aggregates or matrix‑bound complexes under the same assay conditions; (C) need for data demonstrating that the selected exogenous spike‑in truly recapitulates endogenous EV stability and capture behavior through device/formulation stresses and fractionation.
concerns: Detergent/protease protection is an operational (not definitive) indicator of membrane‑enclosed material; some non‑vesicular complexes or tightly bound protein–lipid aggregates can resist these treatments and bind capture reagents, yielding false positives (matches the causal competing explanation e1). Use of orthogonal denaturation/biophysical readouts (e.g., proteomics of captured fractions, lipid profiling, or electron microscopy on fractionated peaks) would reduce this risk.

Assay interference from formulation excipients or device rinse residues could abolish or mask capture signals independent of EV integrity (matching competing explanation e2). Rigorous capture‑compatibility panels and buffer‑matched controls are essential; failure to detect assay incompatibility would confound interpretation.

Spike‑in selection and behavior: an exogenous intact‑EV tracer that differs in surface composition, size distribution, or stability may not faithfully report recovery/performance of endogenous EVs. The plan requires spike‑in validation across buffer/device conditions; otherwise spike‑in recovery may give a false assurance of assay performance.

Species and source differences: prior intranasal positive preclinical outcomes are in mice (ev-zhuang-2011, ev-kodali-2017, ev-hermann-2023) while negative or limited nasal biodistribution was reported in macaques (ev-driedonks-2022). Even if the assay shows preserved surface phenotype ex vivo, this may not predict nasal mucosal clearance, retention in lavage, or negligible brain uptake observed in larger species. The experiment does not resolve cross‑species delivery variability.

Discrimination of alternatives is contingent on multi‑layer orthogonality: particle‑peak co‑localization, spike‑in recovery, and detergent sensitivity must all be met and reproducible across ≥3 independent conditioned‑medium lots. If any single layer is omitted or underpowered, the design will not definitively rule out the competing explanations.

No potency or delivery claim: the proposed identity gate is non‑potency. Without separate functional or in vivo bridging experiments, passing the identity gate should not be interpreted as evidence of preserved biological activity or intranasal CNS delivery.

latestReviewedHypothesis.adversaryObjection: The single strongest bounded failure mode is that assay-positive, detergent-resistant capture signal after device/formulation passage will not reliably report bona fide membrane-protected EVs but instead reflect either (A) non-vesicular, detergent/protease-resistant complexes that bind the chosen capture reagents or (B) assay interference by formulation/device residues — and these alternatives cannot be excluded by the proposed workflow because (1) spike-in tracers may not faithfully mimic endogenous EVs across device/formulation stresses or co-elution behavior, and (2) co-fractionation of aggregates/protein complexes (and species- or device-dependent retention shown in large-animal intranasal work) can produce qualitatively similar readouts even when endogenous EV identity or in vivo delivery competence is lost.
latestReviewedHypothesis.chairRationale: Plausible and implementable as a non‑potency identity gate but lacks direct experimental validation; key gaps must be addressed before CMC use—validated exogenous spike‑in behavior, capture‑compatibility with candidate formulations/device residues, orthogonal evidence to exclude detergent‑resistant non‑vesicular artifacts, and ≥3‑lot reproducibility/scale/device‑relevant testing.
latestReviewedHypothesis.noveltyStatement: Novel: This hypothesis requires concurrent device/formulation passage plus an exogenous intact-EV spike-in internal control applied before exposure, combined with multi-epitope intact immuno-capture, particle-peak co-localization, and detergent/protease protection testing at the fraction level. Prior hypotheses proposed surface-phenotype measurement or in vivo↔ex vivo bridges in isolation; this design uniquely demands spike-in–controlled verification of surface phenotype after realistic device/formulation stresses as a non-potency identity gate. The experiment therefore discriminates true preservation of membrane-protected surface phenotype through delivery-relevant exposures from assay artifacts or secretome-derived artifacts—an operationally new intervention for SGL-001.

reviewerFindings.evidence_gap: Key gaps: (A) lack of direct in vivo linkage showing that preservation of the proposed surface‑phenotype after device/formulation passage predicts in‑host biodistribution or functional/therapeutic readouts; (B) limited orthogonal demonstration that detergent+protease resistance in the chosen capture format cannot be exhibited by non‑vesicular aggregates or matrix‑bound complexes under the same assay conditions; (C) need for data demonstrating that the selected exogenous spike‑in truly recapitulates endogenous EV stability and capture behavior through device/formulation stresses and fractionation.
concerns: Detergent/protease protection is an operational (not definitive) indicator of membrane‑enclosed material; some non‑vesicular complexes or tightly bound protein–lipid aggregates can resist these treatments and bind capture reagents, yielding false positives (matches the causal competing explanation e1). Use of orthogonal denaturation/biophysical readouts (e.g., proteomics of captured fractions, lipid profiling, or electron microscopy on fractionated peaks) would reduce this risk.

Assay interference from formulation excipients or device rinse residues could abolish or mask capture signals independent of EV integrity (matching competing explanation e2). Rigorous capture‑compatibility panels and buffer‑matched controls are essential; failure to detect assay incompatibility would confound interpretation.

Spike‑in selection and behavior: an exogenous intact‑EV tracer that differs in surface composition, size distribution, or stability may not faithfully report recovery/performance of endogenous EVs. The plan requires spike‑in validation across buffer/device conditions; otherwise spike‑in recovery may give a false assurance of assay performance.

Species and source differences: prior intranasal positive preclinical outcomes are in mice (ev-zhuang-2011, ev-kodali-2017, ev-hermann-2023) while negative or limited nasal biodistribution was reported in macaques (ev-driedonks-2022). Even if the assay shows preserved surface phenotype ex vivo, this may not predict nasal mucosal clearance, retention in lavage, or negligible brain uptake observed in larger species. The experiment does not resolve cross‑species delivery variability.

Discrimination of alternatives is contingent on multi‑layer orthogonality: particle‑peak co‑localization, spike‑in recovery, and detergent sensitivity must all be met and reproducible across ≥3 independent conditioned‑medium lots. If any single layer is omitted or underpowered, the design will not definitively rule out the competing explanations.

No potency or delivery claim: the proposed identity gate is non‑potency. Without separate functional or in vivo bridging experiments, passing the identity gate should not be interpreted as evidence of preserved biological activity or intranasal CNS delivery.
